title: The History of Tetris | From A Soviet Computer To Game Boy And Beyond | Gaming History
description: The history of Tetris: Alexey Pajitnov in 1985, the rights race, Henk Rogers and the Game Boy bundle in 1989, The Tetris Company in 1996, Tetris 99 and Tetris Effect.

sections.heading: The puzzle everyone knows
sections.script: Welcome back to the channel. Today we are going through the history of Tetris, probably the most recognised puzzle game in the world. Everyone knows the falling blocks, the satisfying clear of a full line and that famous music. But the story behind the game is just as interesting, because it travels from a Soviet research computer to the Game Boy, through a tangled fight over who owned the rights. We will look at the creator, Alexey Pajitnov, the businessman Henk Rogers, the nineteen eighty nine Game Boy launch, the company that now looks after the game, and the modern versions, like Tetris ninety nine and Tetris Effect. Every date here comes from Wikipedia and from other reference and news pages. Let us start at the beginning.

sections.heading: Alexey Pajitnov builds a game
sections.script: Tetris was created by Alexey Pajitnov, a software engineer working in the Soviet Union. Wikipedia and Britannica both place the creation of the game in nineteen eighty five. The idea came from a puzzle, and the game turned it into a computer challenge: pieces made of four squares fall from the top of the screen, and you rotate and move them to build complete lines. The name combines the Greek word for four with tennis, which was Pajitnov's favourite sport. The first version was very simple, with no complicated levels, and it was passed from person to person on early computers. It spread quickly, because the idea could be understood in just a few seconds.

sections.heading: Reaching the West
sections.script: As copies spread, the game attracted attention outside the Soviet Union. In nineteen eighty eight, Tetris was being shown to the West by the company Spectrum HoloByte, and it was at a trade show in Las Vegas that Henk Rogers first saw it. Rogers was a game publisher who understood immediately that it could be very big. Wikipedia lists the first Western releases in January nineteen eighty eight, from Mirrorsoft in the United Kingdom and Spectrum HoloByte in the United States. The trouble was that the question of who held the rights was very unclear. Several companies had agreed to deals with people who did not fully own the game, and that confusion would shape the next few years.

sections.heading: Henk Rogers goes to Moscow
sections.script: Henk Rogers wanted the handheld rights for Tetris, and he travelled to the Soviet Union in February nineteen eighty nine to deal directly with Elorg, the Soviet state organisation that handled software licensing. His story is the basis of a later film. Rogers believed that Tetris should be included with the Game Boy, a new handheld that Nintendo was preparing. Nintendo's own console, the NES, was also part of the story, because the question of which company could publish Tetris on which system was the heart of the dispute. This was a time when a game could cross a very large political and business gap, and that is part of why the story feels so unusual.

sections.heading: The Game Boy bundle
sections.script: The result was one of the most famous pairings in gaming history. Tetris was released on Game Boy in Japan on the fourteenth of June, nineteen eighty nine, and it came packed in with the Game Boy in North America on the thirty first of July, nineteen eighty nine. Rogers argued that Tetris, and not Super Mario Land, should be the pack in game, because a puzzle game would appeal to everybody and not only to children. That choice was a great success. A game you could play for five minutes on a bus, with a handheld you could put in a pocket, was a perfect match, and the Game Boy became one of the most popular systems of its time.

sections.heading: The legal fight over console rights
sections.script: While the Game Boy version was growing, a legal fight was going on over the console version. According to Wikipedia, the company Tengen released its own NES version of Tetris in nineteen eighty nine, and Nintendo took the matter to court. A judge ruled in Nintendo's favour on the console rights in November nineteen eighty nine, with a formal judgment following in nineteen ninety. This was part of a larger set of disagreements about who was allowed to sell the game on which type of device. It sounds complicated, and it was, but the lesson is simple: Tetris was so popular that everyone wanted the right to sell it, and clear ownership was essential.

sections.heading: The Tetris Company is formed
sections.script: The question of ownership was not settled at once. Nintendo's licence was a limited one, and in nineteen ninety six the rights returned to Pajitnov. Rogers and Pajitnov then formed The Tetris Company to manage licensing for the game, and Wikipedia and other sources agree on this nineteen ninety six date. From that point, the game had a stable home. The Tetris Company decides which games and products may carry the Tetris name, and that is why you see official versions on so many platforms today. It is a rare case of a game creator and a business partner building a long lasting structure around a simple puzzle that began as a hobby project.

sections.heading: Tetris on every screen
sections.script: After the rights were settled, Tetris began to appear almost everywhere: on game consoles, on computers, on mobile phones and in arcades. Many versions added small changes, such as new modes, new music or different piece shapes, but the central idea never changed. That is the secret of the game. It is easy to learn, hard to master, and every round is short and complete. A skilled player and a beginner can both enjoy the same game, and no translation is needed, since the rules are visible on the screen. This is a large part of why Tetris is so often named in lists of the best games ever made, and why it stays a regular topic in these videos.

sections.heading: Tetris ninety nine and Tetris Effect
sections.script: In recent years the game has been reinvented. Tetris Effect, a version that pairs the puzzle with music and light shows, was released on PlayStation four on the ninth of November, twenty eighteen, and on Windows on the twenty third of July, twenty nineteen. Then, on the thirteenth of February, twenty nineteen, Tetris ninety nine was released to Nintendo Switch Online subscribers. It turns Tetris into a battle royale, where ninety nine players compete and send garbage lines to each other. Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa later said that millions of users had played it within a few months. A game from the nineteen eighties found a new life by changing how you play it.

sections.heading: From the games to the screen
sections.script: The story of Tetris became so well known that it was turned into a film. In twenty twenty three, the film called Tetris, a dramatisation of the fight to bring the game out of the Soviet Union, appeared on Apple TV plus, with Taron Egerton playing Henk Rogers. Like any film, it simplifies some events, so the history in this video is based on reference sources and not on the movie. Still, it shows how strong the story is. A tiny game built in the nineteen eighties, passed around by people who simply wanted to play it, became the centre of a business drama and then a film. Few games can say that.

sections.heading: Your Tetris memories
sections.script: That was the history of Tetris, from Alexey Pajitnov's first version in nineteen eighty five to the Game Boy, the rights battles, The Tetris Company and the modern versions. Now we want to hear from you. Where did you first play Tetris? Was it on a Game Boy, on a brick game, on a computer or on your phone? And what is your best score or your favourite version? Tell us in the comments below. If you liked this video, subscribe to the channel and turn on notifications, because we have many more classic game histories coming soon. Thanks so much for watching, and we will see you in the next video.
